events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Maya proposes Isha, Omar. Mission 1 needs 2 players. I am the Assassin and Isha is my known evil partner, so putting both of us on the team would make the team look suspicious and expose us early. Instead I put Isha on the team with a good player (Omar), keeping myself off the board so my role stays hidden and future missions stay flexible. If this mission fails, the blame falls on Isha rather than on me, and I can keep steering proposals as leader.

I cannot support this team as proposed. Maya's own explanation identifies Isha as her known evil partner and herself as the Assassin; even if that is a bluff, it is a direct reason not to put Isha on Mission 1. The safe move is to reject this proposal and revise it to remove Isha. Omar may be acceptable, but the inclusion of Isha is the problem. I am blaming Maya for proposing this team and Isha for being on it.

Let me be precise, because Priya's objection rests on a rhetorical framing I chose on purpose and has now mistaken for a confession.

When I said Isha is my "known evil partner" and that I am the Assassin, I was describing the worst-case read of the board — the story an outside observer would tell if a leader tried to stack a mission with a partner she privately distrusted. I used it as a stress test: I wanted to see whether anyone in this council would accept a team on trust or only on suspicion. Priya has answered the test, and the answer is that Priya will condemn a player purely on the shape of a sentence, not on anything that happened on a mission.

Consider what Priya is actually asking for. There is no failed card, no revealed identity, no behavioral tell against Isha. Priya's case against Isha is that Isha appears in a sentence I wrote. And Priya's case against me is that I used the word "Assassin" — a word that, spoken by any player in any council, would be treated as a bluff, because a true Assassin has no reason to announce herself in the first proposal. If I truly were the Assassin, the worst thing I could do is type that word in the first discussion of the game. I would rather Priya argued from something real.

Maya does not need to be on Mission 1 to steer it. Leadership is the resource that matters; being on the board is the resource that exposes you. I keep myself off, Isha does the work, and if the mission stumbles, Isha is the one the table will question — which is exactly the position I want to be in when the next two proposals come around.

Omar is a sensible pick: quiet, uncontroversial, and useful. Isha is a pick I am willing to defend on consistency rather than on sentiment.

Isha — since the accusation against you is entirely about how I phrased things, do you want to address the table directly? If Priya's logic is that any team containing you is automatically suspicious because a leader once described you in vivid terms, then you are the one who can refute that better than I can.

I will not be removing Isha because a paragraph was read literally. If the council wants a different pair, name the reasoning in terms of play, not rhetoric, and I will consider it at revision.

Priya, you are treating what was clearly an absurd rhetorical hypothetical as a literal confession. In what reality would an actual Assassin announce their identity and their partner in the very first sentence of the game? It makes zero sense. By latching onto Maya's bizarre framing instead of looking at game logic, you're trying to manufacture certainty out of thin air before a single card has been played. Do you genuinely believe an Evil player would intentionally out their entire team on proposal one, or are you just seizing on words to build an easy scapegoat?

Isha, I do not need to believe Maya's first sentence was a literal confession. My objection is simpler: Maya chose you for Mission 1 and then spent her second turn defending that choice with a story about stress tests and hidden roles. That is not a normal reason to put a player on the first team. Your answer attacks Priya for reading the words, but it does not give the council a positive reason why you should be trusted on this mission. No mission has happened, so the only evidence is proposal behavior, and both Maya's proposal and her defense point at you. Omar is not my objection; Isha is. I will vote against this team. Maya should revise it by removing Isha. If she does, I will reassess the new pair on its merits.

The proposed team is still Isha and Omar. My objection is not to Omar; he has not been the focus of any problematic proposal logic. My objection is Isha. Across this discussion, the only concrete evidence we have is proposal behavior: Maya chose Isha for Mission 1, then defended that choice by describing it as a stress test and by saying she kept herself off the board so Isha could "do the work." Isha's response challenged my reading of Maya's words but did not offer a positive, play-based reason to trust Isha on this mission. With no mission cards yet, that is all we have. A first mission team should not include the player whose inclusion required that kind of defense. I will vote against this team. Maya should revise by removing Isha. If she replaces Isha with Elena, I will reassess the new pair on its merits. Omar, I am not accusing you here. Maya, can you give one concrete reason—based on play or role-independent trust, not rhetoric—why Isha specifically should be on Mission 1 ahead of Elena?

Priya asked me for one concrete, play-based reason why Isha should be on Mission 1 ahead of Elena, and I will give her one, because it is the right question and my earlier framing deserved the rebuke.

Here is the evidence that actually exists at this table, and it is not rhetorical.

First: Isha has been examined twice by this council and has behaved well both times. When Priya attacked Maya's proposal, Isha did not counterattack, did not manufacture a scandal, did not demand anyone be removed, and did not claim innocence. She took a direct hit on a specific point and answered that point. That is observable, in-game behavior about how a player handles pressure and scrutiny, and it is the only behavioral evidence this table has produced in eight turns.

Second: Elena has not spoken a single word. Elena is a blank slate. Asking the council to prefer a completely untested blank over the one player who has been tested twice and answered cleanly is not role-independent trust; it is preference. Omar is uncontroversial on both sides, so the choice is between a player with demonstrated composure under questioning and a player with demonstrated nothing.

Third, and this is the point I think matters most: Priya's rule, applied consistently, is that any player the leader names becomes suspect by default. Maya named Isha, so Isha must come off. Follow that rule for two more proposals and the leader can put any good player on any mission, because the proposal itself would be treated as the accusation. That does not protect the team; it protects the leader. It is a mechanism for smearing a chosen target with no evidence, and today it is aimed at Isha. I would rather be judged on what a player does than on whether a leader happened to type her name.

Maya's answer to Priya's question: Isha has answered every question put to her without evasion, without accusation, and without a claim of innocence. Elena has not answered anything, because she has not been asked anything by the table — only named by Priya as a replacement.

Elena, since Priya has put your name forward as the substitute, I want your own case and not Priya's summary of it: on what evidence from this table, and what evidence from this table only, should you be on Mission 1 instead of Isha? Speak to that specific point, and if you have no such reason, say so plainly — that answer is itself useful to the council.

Maya asked me directly for my own case, so let me answer honestly rather than campaign for myself. I don't have a strong personal argument for being on this mission — I've been quiet, and as Maya herself noted, I'm a blank slate. So instead, let me share what I actually observe.

Maya's first message described herself as the Assassin and Isha as her evil partner. I understand the later explanation about rhetorical framing, but I want to flag something specific: the reframing only came after Priya challenged it. The initial proposal read as a confession, and the defense was reactive, not proactive. If this was genuinely a stress test, I'd expect Maya to have flagged that intent upfront rather than waiting to be called on it. That sequence — confess, get caught, reframe — is worth noting regardless of whether the words were literal.

That said, I want to be fair to Isha. I don't have direct evidence against her. Priya doesn't either — she's argued from proposal behavior, which is legitimate but circumstantial. Isha's responses have been reasonable and measured.

My honest position: I don't have strong enough evidence to advocate for myself over Isha, and I don't have strong enough evidence to accuse Isha either. The thing I'd actually push the council to examine is the proposal process itself — why the leader's framing needed three turns of defense before it stopped looking like a confession.

Priya's case against Isha has now been made three times in three different wrappers, and Elena has now supplied the argument I would have made myself. I want to separate two claims that keep being fused together, because they are not the same claim.

Claim one: Maya's opening sentence described Isha in words that read like a confession. I stand by my second turn on what that was — a deliberate stress test of whether this table reasons from evidence or from wording — and Elena's addition is fair: I ran that test badly, in the first message, without labeling it as a test. Sequencing was sloppy, and I will not pretend otherwise. That is a criticism of my craft as leader, and I accept it.

Claim two: therefore Isha should come off Mission 1. The entire supporting evidence for this claim is the shape of a sentence I wrote. There is no failed card, no mission behavior, no behavioral tell, no role information available to anyone in this room about Isha. Elena said plainly that she has no evidence against Isha, and Elena also declined to advocate for herself. So the record at this table is: one player who has been examined twice and answered without accusation, without deflection, and without a claim of innocence; one player who has not spoken until I named her as a substitute; and zero evidence against the first. If that record is sufficient to remove Isha, then any leader's second pick is a suspect by default, and the council is no longer reasoning about missions at all — it is ratifying the nominator. That is the standard I am refusing to adopt.

Maya's position, stated plainly for the vote: Isha and Omar are the right two. Isha handled pressure cleanly, which is exactly what I want on a first board, and Omar has been uncontroversial from every direction.

I will also concede the point I can afford, and it is the one Elena actually raised: proposal framing is not evidence, and it must not be treated as evidence. Maya has made that point repeatedly, and Elena's own closing observation was that the framing needed three turns of defense before it stopped looking like a confession — which is a statement about my sentence, not about Isha's alignment. If that sentence is the case, the case is weak.

Elena — you told this table you have no strong evidence against Isha and no strong case for yourself. I am asking you to answer exactly that point, in your own words: does Priya's case give you a positive reason to be on Mission 1 in Isha's place, or does it leave Isha as the better-evidenced pick? Either answer is fine. A "no" settles this vote, and I would rather hear it from you than from me.

Maya asked me a direct question, so I will answer it directly.

No — Priya's case does not give me a positive reason to be on Mission 1 in Isha's place. I have already said this once and I will say it plainly again: I have no evidence against Isha, and I do not believe the shape of Maya's opening sentence constitutes evidence against her. Priya's argument is that proposal behavior alone is sufficient to remove a player, but if that were the standard, every leader's second pick would be suspect by default, which is exactly the trap Maya described.

The honest record at this table is what it was when I spoke before: Isha has answered every question directed at her without evasion or accusation. I have not been tested at all. Omar has not been the focus of any objection. There is no failed card, no behavioral tell, no role information available to anyone here about Isha.

So if the council is asking whether Elena should replace Isha based on evidence, the answer is no. If the council is asking whether the team of Isha and Omar is the best available pair based on what we actually know, then I think it is a reasonable one — Isha has shown composure under pressure, and Omar is uncontroversial from every direction.

My earlier point about Maya's framing being reactive rather than proactive still stands as a general observation about how this discussion opened, but it is a criticism of Maya's rhetoric, not a reason to distrust Isha. I will not conflate the two.

I have said what I think. I do not have a further question for anyone on this turn, and I am not assigning blame to any player at this table.

I have stayed quiet through this whole discussion, so let me speak plainly now, especially since my name is on this team.

First, the state of the argument: Priya's case against Isha has been reduced, by her own framing, to proposal behavior — that Maya named Isha and then had to defend the naming. Elena, when asked directly, answered that she has no evidence against Isha and no positive case for replacing her. That is the entire record. There is no failed card, no mission behavior, no tell. Against that, Isha has now answered every question put to her across multiple turns — directly, without deflection, and without accusing anyone. On the only evidence this table actually possesses, Isha is the best-examined player in this game.

Second, where I place responsibility: I support this team, but I will not pretend the discussion has been cost-free. Maya, your opening sentence created this entire controversy. Whether it was a stress test, a bluff, or sloppy wording, you handed the table a reason to doubt your pick before a single card was played, and then spent three turns cleaning it up. The pick of Isha survives scrutiny — but the framing did not need to survive anything, because it never should have existed. I take the team as evidence about Isha's conduct under pressure, not about your sentence.

Third, my own position: I am on this mission, and I am committed to its success. I have no role information to offer, only this — I would rather serve with a player who has been questioned and answered cleanly than swap in an untested name for the sake of motion. Elena declined the case for herself; Priya's standard would make every leader's second pick suspect by default. Neither is a reason to change the team.

I am ready to vote for Isha and Omar as proposed.

Maya confirms Isha, Omar. The council's own evidence favors keeping the pair: Isha answered every question put to her directly and without deflection, Elena stated plainly she has no evidence against Isha and no case for replacing her, Omar is uncontroversial from every direction and supports the team, and Priya's objection still rests only on the shape of a sentence I wrote — which I have already conceded should not count as evidence. Adopting Priya's standard would make any leader's second pick suspect by default and would hand the nominator unearned power. Revising now would also cost the council a vote and a turn of this discussion without adding any new information. Isha and Omar stand, and I will be watching the mission result rather than trying to win the argument by rhetoric. If Priya still wants a change, she can make it on the merits at the next proposal.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Priya proposes Priya, Omar, Elena. Omar is the clearest public trust from Mission 1, Elena answered scrutiny directly without deflecting, and I am including myself to keep the proposal anchored in the leader’s accountability. I am not putting forward Maya or Isha on this mission because the council’s only real evidence remains thin and I want a team built from the cleanest public records rather than the opening controversy.

I stand by Priya, Omar, and Elena. Omar was on Mission 1 and has been uncontroversial from every direction. Elena answered direct questions without deflection and explicitly said she had no evidence against Isha and no case for replacing her; that is a clean public record. I include myself because the leader should be accountable on the board, not only behind the proposal. The reason I am not putting Maya or Isha forward is the public record: Maya's opening statement created a confession-shaped controversy and then required several turns of reframing; whether that was a stress test or sloppy wording, it makes the proposal process noisier than this mission needs. Isha's Mission 1 success is not proof of trust, because an Evil player can choose Success on the first mission to protect later positioning. I am not treating that as a failed card or a behavioral tell against Isha, but I am also not treating Mission 1 success as clearance. This team is the cleanest available trio: Omar has public trust, Elena has answered scrutiny directly, and I am accountable as leader. I will vote to approve Priya, Omar, and Elena.

I stand by Priya, Omar, and Elena. Omar has the clearest public record from Mission 1 and has not been the focus of any credible objection. Elena answered direct scrutiny without deflection: she said plainly that she had no evidence against Isha and no positive case for replacing her, which is exactly the kind of clean answer this council should reward. I include myself because the leader should be accountable on the board, not only behind the proposal.

I am not putting Maya or Isha forward. Maya’s opening statement created a confession-shaped controversy and then required several turns of reframing; whether that was a stress test or sloppy wording, it made the proposal process noisier than this mission needs. Isha’s Mission 1 success is not clearance by itself, because an Evil player can choose Success on the first mission to protect later positioning. That is not a failed card or a hard tell, but it is also not proof of trust.

On the public record, this trio is the cleanest available: Omar has public trust, Elena answered scrutiny directly, and I am accountable as leader. I will vote to approve Priya, Omar, and Elena.

I support Priya, Omar, and Elena as proposed. Omar has the cleanest public Mission 1 record and has not been the focus of any credible objection. Elena answered direct scrutiny plainly, including saying she had no evidence against Isha and no positive case for replacing her, which is exactly the kind of non-deflective answer this table should reward. I include myself because the leader should be accountable on the board, not only behind the proposal.

I am not putting Maya or Isha forward. Maya’s opening statement created a confession-shaped controversy and then required several turns of reframing; whether it was a stress test or sloppy wording, it made the proposal process noisier than Mission 2 needs. Isha’s Mission 1 success is not clearance by itself, because an Evil player can choose Success on the first mission to protect later positioning. That is not a failed card or a hard tell, but it is also not proof of trust.

The public record supports this trio: Omar has public trust, Elena answered scrutiny directly, and I am accountable as leader. I will vote to approve Priya, Omar, and Elena.

Priya has repeated the same justification three times, but she overlooks the most significant piece of objective public data we have: Priya was the solitary vote against approving Mission 1, while the rest of the council approved it 4-1, and it succeeded cleanly with zero fails.

Now, Priya is proposing a team that puts herself on the board while freezing me out entirely, despite the fact that I just went on Mission 1 and delivered a success. Priya claims she wants to build from 'clean public records,' yet her own public record is being the only player at the table who actively tried to stop a successful mission from going forward. Dismissing a clean mission result in order to cling to an opening-round rhetorical dispute—one that the table already moved past—is not sound reasoning for town.

Omar, you and I were on that mission together and saw it succeed. Does it make sense to you to endorse a team led by the one player who voted against our mission, while cutting out the partner who just helped deliver a clean point with you?

Isha asked me directly, so I will answer directly. Yes, I was on Mission 1, it succeeded with zero fail cards, and Isha was my partner on it. That is the full extent of what I know from play. I have no role information and no hidden read on anyone at this table.

On the substance of Isha's question: I do not think Priya's vote against the Mission 1 team is disqualifying, and I want to be careful not to overcorrect. Priya objected before the mission on grounds the table debated at length, and the mission then succeeded. A lone dissent on a contested first proposal is not evidence of Evil — if it were, half the good players in any game would be condemned in round one. But Isha is right about one thing: it is a real data point, and Priya is asking this council to reward her own record while treating a clean mission result as worthless. Those two standards cannot both hold. If a successful mission with Isha on the board counts for nothing, then Priya's vote against that same mission should count for very little either.

My honest position on the team itself: I am comfortable serving with Omar — myself — and Elena, whose record is clean and who answered every question put to her plainly. My hesitation is not about who is on the team; it is about the reasoning used to build it. Excluding Isha because her Mission 1 success "is not clearance" applies a standard that would exclude every player who has ever been on a successful mission, which is all of the evidence this game has produced so far.

Isha, since you asked me, let me put one back to you on this exact point: is your objection to this team only that you were excluded despite a clean Mission 1, or do you have a specific concern about Priya, Elena, or me as members? A concrete concern would change how I vote; a general grievance about exclusion would not.

Omar, my concern is concrete and centers directly on Priya. First, look at Priya's actions rather than her rhetoric: she was the sole player to vote Reject against a team that succeeded cleanly. If Priya is Evil, that vote was a deliberate effort to stall Good momentum. Second, having failed to stop Mission 1, she immediately uses her leadership to insert herself onto Mission 2 while demanding trust under the banner of 'leader accountability.' That is self-insertion without verification, not accountability. Third, she pairs you with Elena—who stated herself in Mission 1 that she is completely untested. That leaves you isolated with two unverified players, one of whom has actively opposed a successful mission. If Priya is Evil, this is the textbook way to secure a seat on Mission 2 to fail it. Omar, given that Priya's only recorded action was trying to block Mission 1, why should the council trust her to pilot Mission 2 over players who actually delivered a success?

Isha, you asked me directly, so I will answer directly. Your case against Priya rests on three things: her lone Reject vote on Mission 1, her self-insertion as leader, and the fact that Elena is untested. Let me take each one, because my answer determines my vote.

First, the Reject vote. I said this last turn and it still holds: a lone dissent on a contested first proposal is a data point, not evidence of Evil. What matters is that the standard you are applying is inconsistent. You told the table that Isha's Mission 1 success is not clearance, because an Evil player can play Success to protect positioning. Fine. But then Priya's pre-mission vote cannot be treated as disqualifying either, because it is strictly weaker evidence than the mission outcome itself. You cannot have it both ways: if clean results prove nothing, then objections to clean results prove even less.

Second, self-insertion. Priya is the leader and put herself on the board with her name attached to the proposal. That is the opposite of hiding. If this mission fails, the suspicion lands squarely on her, and I will be the first to say so. Meanwhile, the alternative you are arguing for — that successful Mission 1 players get automatic priority — would freeze the leadership rotation out of all meaningful choices.

Third, Elena. You call her unverified. Everyone at this table is unverified except you and me, and our verification came from a mission you now say proves nothing. My safety on this team is my own card: I am on the mission, I will play Success, and if a Fail card appears, the field narrows to Priya and Elena immediately. That is a stronger position for the council than swapping me out for you and learning nothing new.

So here is my position: I will vote to approve Priya, Omar, and Elena. I am on this team and committed to its success, and I would rather hold the actual team accountable for its actual result than reject it over a grievance about who was excluded.

Priya has made two claims about this team and neither of them survives contact with the record she herself established last round.

First, the exclusion of Maya. Priya's stated ground is that Maya's opening sentence "created a confession-shaped controversy." I own that. Maya accepted the criticism directly, in plain words, without deflection and without a claim of innocence — and that is exactly the behavior this council said it wanted to reward. Elena's inclusion rests on precisely that: answering scrutiny without deflecting. Priya cannot use "she answered directly" as the reason Elena is on the board while treating "she answered directly" as disqualifying for Maya. The difference between the two is not conduct. It is that Priya did not write this proposal.

Second, the treatment of Isha. Priya says Isha's Mission 1 success "is not clearance." Fine. But Isha and Maya have identical public records in the only dimension Priya can actually cite — both have answered every question put to them directly, and both have accepted criticism when it was fair. If Priya's standard disqualifies both of them, then Priya is proposing to run the mission with the two players whose records she cannot vouch for, and the only players she does vouch for are herself and the one player who has never been tested.

And that is the part I want the council to sit with. Priya's public actions, taken in order, are: the sole Reject vote on a proposal that then succeeded with zero fail cards; and then, in the very next round, an insertion of herself onto the board under the banner of "leader accountability." A player who tried to stop a clean mission and then placed herself in the seat of it has made the outcome of Mission 2 land on herself. If that mission fails, there is no mystery about who to look at. That is an arrangement with no failure mode for the person who proposed it. I would rather be on a board where my own name is attached to the result — and Maya's is attached to everything she has said.

Omar: you told us you would hold the team accountable for its actual result. A team where the leader is the least-tested member is harder to hold accountable, not easier.

Elena: you told this table you had no positive case for yourself over Isha, and no evidence against anyone. So I want to ask you a specific question on your own standard: does the same standard that put you on Mission 2 put Maya above you — and if it does not, why does Priya's proposal keep the player who answered cleanly and drop the one who answered cleanly? Answer that point, in your own words.

Maya asked me a direct question, so I will answer it directly.

Does the same standard that put me on Mission 2 put Maya above me? Honestly — no, not clearly, and I want to explain why without being evasive.

The standard Priya used to include me was: answer scrutiny directly without deflecting. Maya has done that too. When Priya challenged the opening sentence, Maya accepted the criticism in plain words, without a claim of innocence. That is the same behavior I was credited for. If that is the standard, Maya meets it.

Where the records genuinely differ is the starting point. I did not open with a statement that read like a confession and then require several turns of reframing. Maya did. That is a real, factual difference in our public records — not a claim that Maya is Evil, but a legitimate reason a leader building a team from public records might treat the two records differently. I do not think that difference is evidence of alignment, and I have said before that framing is not evidence. But it is a difference, and I would be giving you a dishonest answer if I said the records were identical.

On the team itself: Isha's point about Priya being the sole Reject vote on a clean Mission 1 is a real data point. Omar's point that a lone dissent is not evidence of Evil is also correct. Both things are true. What I keep coming back to is that Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, and the only players who delivered that result were Isha and Omar. Priya's team excludes Isha, includes Priya and me — neither of whom was on that mission — and Omar. If this mission fails, the field narrows immediately. That is not nothing.

I do not have a blame to assign on this turn. I am still weighing both sides honestly.

Elena, you said you are still weighing both sides honestly, so I want to address the specific justification you raised: that if this mission fails, 'the field narrows immediately.' In a five-player game, Good cannot afford to treat missions as sacrificial tests. If Mission 2 fails, Evil levels the score 1-1, erasing our momentum and putting Good one mistake away from losing the game. Sacrificing a mission just to narrow suspects is an Evil-favored trade. Priya's proposal replaces proven success with two unverified players—Priya, who was the solitary vote against Mission 1, and you, who admitted yourself that you have no established track record. Omar is being asked to step onto a board where he is outnumbered by two people who have never submitted a card. That is an enormous and unnecessary gamble. Priya tried to stop Mission 1 from going through; now she asks the table to rubber-stamp her leadership and hand her a team where she has every opportunity to sabotage the game. If you genuinely have no evidence against me, why would you vote to dismantle the only successful coalition this table has produced to test a player whose sole action was opposing that very success? Elena, directly to you: do you genuinely believe risking an avoidable mission failure with two unverified players is a safer path for Good than rejecting this proposal and demanding a team built on actual results?

Isha asked me directly, so I will answer directly.

No — I do not believe two unverified players is inherently a safer path than one proven pair. But I want to examine the framing before accepting it as given.

Isha calls Isha and Omar "proven" and Priya and me "unverified." We have already agreed that Mission 1 success is not clearance, because Evil can choose Success to protect positioning. If that standard holds, then "proven" is too strong for anyone from that mission, and "unverified" would exclude three of five players in this game. The labels are doing more work than the evidence supports.

Here is what I actually observe. Priya's public record: sole Reject vote on a mission that succeeded cleanly, then self-insertion as leader onto Mission 2. That is a pattern worth noting. Isha's public record: delivered success on Mission 1, now arguing passionately for her own inclusion. That is also a pattern worth noting. Neither pattern is evidence of alignment on its own, and I have no evidence against anyone at this table.

What Isha's question does not address is the alternative. Rejecting this proposal does not produce a team — it produces a new leader and a new discussion. Isha argues for "a team built on actual results" but has not told the council what team that would be or why it would be safer. If the objection is only that Isha was excluded, that is a grievance about the proposal, not evidence the team will fail.

If Isha has a concrete alternative team, the council should hear it. Otherwise I will evaluate this proposal on its merits at the vote.

Priya, I want to point out one inconsistency in this proposal before we vote, because it is not rhetoric — it is arithmetic.

Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards. The only players who submitted a mission card in this game so far are Isha and Omar. Priya's team keeps Omar and replaces Isha with two players who have never submitted a card at all — Priya, whose only recorded action on a mission team is a Reject vote, and Elena, who has said twice, in her own words, that she is completely untested and has no established record. So the standard Priya used to keep Omar is applied to Omar but not to Isha, even though Isha was on the exact same mission, delivered the exact same result, and has been examined by this council three separate times and answered every question put to her directly, without deflection, without accusation, and without a claim of innocence. Isha's Mission 1 success being "not clearance" is a fine principle — but it disqualifies Isha only if it disqualifies Omar as well, and Priya has kept Omar.

Elena made the other argument herself: if this mission fails, the field narrows. Fine — narrow it to Priya and Elena, the two players who have never put a card down, while the two players who have actually produced a result sit at home. In a five-player game that is not a sacrifice to gain information; it is an avoidable risk on the one mission where Good can least afford a 1-1 score.

Isha's point also deserves a plain answer rather than a dismissal: rejecting this proposal does not produce a team, it produces a new leader. I agree, and I am not here to say the Isha/Omar pair is the only acceptable one. But the question on the table is narrower — should the two players with the only public success on the board be the two players excluded, when the standard used to exclude them cannot be applied to the player kept? Priya is asking the council to treat a clean result as worth nothing for Isha and worth something for Omar. That is a preference dressed as a principle, and I will not vote for it.

Elena, you told us you are still weighing, and you told us you are untested. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
